arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Cahn argued that Congress intended to end the practice of sending defendants to prison for treatment.
Mr. Bibas argued that the Sentencing Reform Act rejected unstructured sentencing procedures designed to confine inmates indefinitely.
Mr. Roberts stated that Section 3582(a) prohibits courts from lengthening imprisonment to promote rehabilitation.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case examines the limits of judicial sentencing power. The core issue is whether the Sentencing Reform Act bars judges from using prison time as a tool to secure rehabilitation services.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the sentence reduced because the judge used prison time to secure treatment.
The government wants the sentence to stand because judges may consider treatment needs when setting terms.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that Congress banned using imprisonment to promote rehabilitation or secure treatment access.
The government argues that judges may consider needed treatments when deciding whether to imprison and for how long.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor asked if the judge’s focus on crime seriousness contradicted the treatment rationale.
Justice Scalia asked if the defendant received the treatment the judge intended to secure.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between punishment and rehabilitation in federal sentencing. It clarifies whether judges can use prison terms to guarantee access to specific correctional programs. The outcome shapes how courts balance public safety with individual treatment needs.
